prize_parts.citation: for the design and formulation of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable systemic delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: My preferred achievement is unchanged: ionizable lipid nanoparticles as the molecular-design solution to nucleic-acid delivery. The chemistry can be stated in a sentence (a lipid that is near neutral in blood and charged in the acidified endosome, assembled with nucleic acid under controlled mixing into a particle that encapsulates efficiently and releases its cargo), it is supported by quantitative physical chemistry (pKa tuning, packing and phase behaviour), and it has been independently reproduced for decades. The test I weigh most, whether researchers and clinicians can now do something they could not, is met in the strongest form: an approved siRNA drug, mRNA vaccines at global scale, and now in vivo gene-editing payloads. After round 1 I have changed one thing, the third name. I now propose Cullis, Madden and Hope rather than Anderson, because the first approved product and the formulation platform used for the vaccines trace through the Vancouver encapsulation and ionizable-lipid line, and the decisive step the chair asks about looks to me like that line and not the later lipidoid screening.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakest point: MacLachlan (clinical-scale siRNA-LNP) and the Anderson-Langer lipidoid line have real claims that a three-name limit leaves out, and I have not verified patent and priority details. There is also a genuine risk that colleagues read this as pharmaceutical formulation instead of chemistry, and that the 2023 Medicine prize makes the area feel already honoured. B056 has a wider base of support and a clearer protein-level mechanism, so I accept that my configuration currently trails it in count; I do not treat counts as evidence, but I do owe the committee a statement of what would move me.

responses.point: Sparr proposes Cullis, Madden and Hope, grounding B019 in lipid phase behaviour and attributing the decisive formulation work to the Vancouver group, and says that if the decisive step were library design her choice would shift towards Anderson.
responses.response: You have persuaded me on the third name. In round 1 I kept Anderson for the lipidoid screening line, but the chair's question forces me to ask which line the approved products actually descend from, and the answer is the Vancouver ionizable-lipid and encapsulation work. Anderson and Langer made an important and independent contribution to lipid discovery, but I cannot say it was the decisive step for patisiran or the first mRNA vaccines, so I move to your trio. I share your concern that we both lean on a phase-behaviour explanation, so I would write the citation around design and formulation of the particles and not around one physical mechanism.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B056 first as a general catalytic way to remove any protein, with cereblon explaining thalidomide, and keeps B019 as his fallback.
responses.response: Your fallback ranking of B019 matters to me, because it means that on the scientific case we are closer than the counts suggest. I still think the maturity asymmetry is real: LNPs have decades of clinical vindication, while the PROTAC branch has no approved drug and the approved glue branch is a different line from the one Crews and Deshaies opened. If the committee insists on B056 I would want the citation to be honest that it covers two lines, but I would rather you move to B019 than have us force a three-name citation over Ciulli and Sakamoto.

responses.point: Zou moved from perovskites to B056 on the strength of ternary-complex crystal structures, many independent reproductions and breadth of support, while conceding that waiting may be wiser.
responses.response: I accept that the structural evidence for ternary complexes is a strong, physical argument and that I undervalued it in round 1. But you also say yourself that the heterobifunctional branch awaits clinical proof, and that is the criterion that separates the two candidates for me. What would move me toward B056 is an approved PROTAC or an expert report that treats the induced-proximity concept as complete; absent that, I would sooner reward a platform already delivering medicines.

responses.point: Brzezinski supports B056 with Crews, Deshaies and Handa because each name maps to a distinct attributable step, so the three-person limit works without a priority ranking.
responses.response: That is the strongest attribution argument for B056 and I cannot match its tidiness for B019, where credit is more entangled. But tidy credit is not the same as a settled achievement: your own case_against concedes that Handa's cereblon work and the PROTAC concept are two lines that a citation must hold together without implying a single discovery. I would rather accept a harder attribution problem for a result that is unambiguously complete than an easy trio over a concept whose clinical verdict is still pending.

uncertainties: Whether Hope or Madden should be displaced by MacLachlan, Anderson or Langer, and what the priority record shows once patents and early papers are checked.
Whether a majority sees LNP delivery as chemistry (molecular design and self-assembly) or as pharmaceutical formulation, and whether the 2023 Medicine prize weighs against it.
Whether PROTAC clinical readouts in the coming years will make B056 the more defensible choice, and whether I am too conservative about timing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict or recusal need regarding any shortlisted candidate. My postdoc mentors (Molly Stevens, Freddy Boey) and my Linkoping biosensor and peptide work have no link to the credited names. I share a self-assembly perspective and an interest in nanoparticle biomedicine with Emma Sparr, which I regard as a shared scientific viewpoint and not a recusal issue.
